Multivariate QTL Mapping with wgAim

Julian Taylor & Ari Verbyla

2026-05-23

Source: vignettes/qtlAim_mv_pipeline.qmd

1 Overview

This vignette demonstrates the multivariate extension of the wgAim QTL mapping pipeline for a biparental mapping population evaluated across multiple environments. The framework detects QTL that act consistently across environments (main-effect QTL) as well as QTL whose effects differ between environments (G×E interaction QTL), within a unified forward-selection model.

The pipeline has the same three stages as the univariate analysis:

  1. Pre-analysis — prepare the wgCross object using primeCross().
  2. Analysis — develop a multi-environment base model and run qtlAim() with the Trait argument to activate the multivariate engine.
  3. Post-analysis — interrogate, summarise, and visualise the detected QTL using summary(), plot(), and aimTrace().

Throughout we use the genoMVsim and phenoMVsim datasets bundled with the package: a simulated Doubled Haploid (DH) population of 120 lines genotyped at 600 markers across 6 chromosomes, evaluated in 8 field trials with 2 replicates each. Four QTL were planted: two with consistent effects across trials (main effect) and two with environment-specific effects (G×E).

Requires: ASReml-R V4. The vignette is pre-rendered so no licence is needed to read it. Run the code chunks only if you have ASReml-R installed.

2 Mathematical Framework

2.1 The multivariate linear mixed model

Let t=1,…,Tt = 1, \ldots, T index environments (trials) and let 𝐲t\boldsymbol{y}_t be the n×1n \times 1 vector of phenotypic observations for environment tt. The stacked response across all environments is 𝐲=(𝐲1⊤,…,𝐲T⊤)⊤\boldsymbol{y} = (\boldsymbol{y}_1^\top, \ldots, \boldsymbol{y}_T^\top)^\top. The base linear mixed model is

𝐲=𝐗𝛕+𝐙u𝐮+𝐙g𝐠+𝐞, \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\tau} + \boldsymbol{Z}_u\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{g} + \boldsymbol{e},

where 𝐗\boldsymbol{X} and 𝐙u\boldsymbol{Z}_u are design matrices for the fixed effects 𝛕\boldsymbol{\tau} (environment means, replicate effects) and peripheral random effects 𝐮\boldsymbol{u} respectively, and 𝐞∼𝒩(𝟎,𝚺e)\boldsymbol{e} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e) with 𝚺e\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_e a block-diagonal residual structure allowing environment-specific error variances. The genetic line effects 𝐠\boldsymbol{g} are modelled jointly across environments as

𝐠∼𝒩(𝟎,𝐆a⊗𝐈n), \boldsymbol{g} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\boldsymbol{0},\, \boldsymbol{G}_a \otimes \boldsymbol{I}_n\right),

where 𝐆a\boldsymbol{G}_a is the T×TT \times T genetic (co)variance matrix capturing the magnitude of genetic variation in each environment and the genetic correlations between environments.

2.2 Factor analytic structure for 𝐆a\boldsymbol{G}_a

With many environments, 𝐆a\boldsymbol{G}_a has T(T+1)/2T(T+1)/2 free parameters — too many to estimate reliably unless the number of lines is large. A parsimonious and biologically interpretable approximation is the factor analytic (FA) model of order kk:

𝐆a=𝚲𝚲⊤+𝚿, \boldsymbol{G}_a = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^\top + \boldsymbol{\Psi},

where 𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda} is the T×kT \times k matrix of factor loadings and 𝚿=diag(ψ1,…,ψT)\boldsymbol{\Psi} = \text{diag}(\psi_1, \ldots, \psi_T) is a diagonal matrix of environment-specific specific variances. The loadings capture the dominant axes of genotype-by-environment interaction, while the specific variances absorb any residual environment-specific genetic variation not explained by the common factors. An FA(kk) model has Tk+T=T(k+1)Tk + T = T(k+1) parameters, which is much smaller than the full T(T+1)/2T(T+1)/2 when k≪Tk \ll T.

2.3 Introducing additive genetic effects

As in the univariate case, the genetic term 𝐠\boldsymbol{g} is decomposed into an additive composite term 𝐚\boldsymbol{a} — representing the cumulative effect of all markers across the genome — and a residual polygenic term 𝐩\boldsymbol{p} that absorbs genetic signal not captured by any detected QTL:

𝐲=𝐗𝛕+𝐙u𝐮+𝐙g𝐚+𝐙g𝐩+𝐞. \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\tau} + \boldsymbol{Z}_u\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{p} + \boldsymbol{e}.

The composite additive term uses one of two equivalent computational paths depending on the ratio of marker intervals pp to lines nn:

  • vm path (p>np > n): The aggregate marker signal is absorbed into a genomic relationship matrix 𝐊=1p𝐌𝐌⊤\boldsymbol{K} = \tfrac{1}{p}\boldsymbol{M}\boldsymbol{M}^{\top}, and 𝐚∼𝒩(𝟎,𝐆a⊗𝐊)\boldsymbol{a} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\, \boldsymbol{G}_a \otimes \boldsymbol{K}). This is the multivariate extension of the standard GBLUP formulation, efficient when there are more intervals than lines.
  • mbf path (n≥pn \geq p): Each marker effect is treated as an independent random regression coefficient, 𝐚=(𝐈T⊗𝐌)𝐪\boldsymbol{a} = (\boldsymbol{I}_T \otimes \boldsymbol{M})\boldsymbol{q} with 𝐪∼𝒩(𝟎,𝐆a⊗σq2𝐈p)\boldsymbol{q} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\, \boldsymbol{G}_a \otimes \sigma^2_q\,\boldsymbol{I}_p). This path is preferred when lines outnumber intervals.

Both paths yield identical QTL selection results. The engine selects the appropriate path automatically; the force = TRUE argument overrides to the mbf path. In this vignette, with 594 intervals and 120 lines (p>np > n), the vm path is used throughout, and 𝐆a\boldsymbol{G}_a carries the same factor analytic structure as the base model.

2.4 Forward selection and the likelihood ratio test

Forward selection proceeds identically to the univariate case. At each iteration a likelihood ratio test (LRT) is used to determine whether any interval or marker carries significant additive signal. For TT environments, however, each candidate is tested as a TT-vector of fixed effects — one per environment — so the test statistic follows a chi-squared mixture distribution rather than a standard χ12\chi^2_1:

Λ=−2(ℓreduced−ℓfull)∼approx.∑j=0Twjχj2, \Lambda = -2\!\left(\ell_{\text{reduced}} - \ell_{\text{full}}\right) \;\stackrel{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; \sum_{j=0}^{T} w_j \,\chi^2_j,

where the mixing weights wj=(Tj)12Tw_j = \binom{T}{j} \tfrac{1}{2^T} arise from the boundary constraints on variance components, and ℓ\ell is the restricted log-likelihood. The mixture critical value at family-wise significance level TypeI is obtained numerically via qchisq.mixture().

2.5 Genome-wide outlier statistic

Because the BLUP of interval kk’s additive effect is now a TT-vector 𝐪̃k\tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k, the outlier statistic is a quadratic form in 𝐆a−1\boldsymbol{G}_a^{-1}:

ok=𝐪̃k⊤𝐆a−1𝐪̃kṽk, o_k = \frac{\tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k^\top\, \boldsymbol{G}_a^{-1}\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k}{\tilde{v}_k},

where the normalising scalar ṽk=tr(𝐆a−1𝐓k𝐕̃𝐚𝐓k⊤)\tilde{v}_k = \text{tr}\!\left(\boldsymbol{G}_a^{-1}\, \boldsymbol{T}_k\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{a}}\, \boldsymbol{T}_k^\top\right), 𝐓k=𝐈T⊗𝐭k⊤\boldsymbol{T}_k = \boldsymbol{I}_T \otimes \boldsymbol{t}_k^\top is the extraction matrix for interval kk, and 𝐕̃𝐚\tilde{\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{a}} is the posterior variance matrix of the composite random term. This statistic is non-negative and approximately chi-squared scaled, placing all intervals on a common scale regardless of the number of environments.

2.6 Post-selection: main-effect vs G×E QTL

After all QTL have been selected, a Wald zero-equality test is applied to the TT-vector of fixed effects for each detected QTL. QTL whose effects are consistent across environments (main effects) are retained with a single fixed coefficient; those with significant environment-specific variation are retained as a full TT-vector of environment-specific effects (G×E interaction QTL). The final model is

𝐲=𝐗𝛕+𝐙g∑j∈ℳβ̂j𝐱j+𝐙g∑k∈ℐ𝛄̂k⊤𝐱k+𝐙u𝐮+𝐙g𝐚−s+𝐙g𝐩+𝐞, \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\tau} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\!\sum_{j \in \mathcal{M}} \hat{\beta}_j\,\boldsymbol{x}_j + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\!\sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}} \hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}_k^\top\,\boldsymbol{x}_k + \boldsymbol{Z}_u\boldsymbol{u} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{a}_{-s} + \boldsymbol{Z}_g\boldsymbol{p} + \boldsymbol{e},

where 𝐚−s=𝐌−s𝐪−s\boldsymbol{a}_{-s} = \boldsymbol{M}_{-s}\boldsymbol{q}_{-s} where the 𝐌−s\boldsymbol{M}_{-s} denotes 𝐌\boldsymbol{M} with an omission of markers/intervals in the windows of the QTL selected; ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes main-effect QTL with scalar effects $_j and ℐ\mathcal{I} denotes G×E QTL with environment-specific effect vectors 𝛄̂k\hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}_k.

3 Data Preparation — primeCross() 

data(genoMVsim,  package = "wgAim")
data(phenoMVsim, package = "wgAim")

primeCross() converts the cross object into a wgCross object with interval genotype scores ready for qtlAim():

genObj <- primeCross(genoMVsim, type = "interval", id = "id")
n_chr <- length(genObj$geno)
n_int <- sum(sapply(genObj$geno, function(ch) ncol(ch$interval.data)))
n_mk  <- sum(sapply(genObj$geno, function(ch) ncol(ch$data)))
cat(sprintf("Chromosomes : %d\n", n_chr))
cat(sprintf("Markers     : %d\n", n_mk))
cat(sprintf("Intervals   : %d\n", n_int))
cat(sprintf("Lines       : %d\n", nrow(genObj$pheno)))

With 594 intervals and 120 lines, the ratio p/n>1p/n > 1 and qtlAim() will automatically use the vm (genomic relationship matrix) engine path.

4 Base Model Development

The starting point for a multivariate analysis is a converged multi-environment base model that captures the experimental design structure and the genetic (co)variance across environments. We build this incrementally, comparing three variance structures for the genetic term.

phenoMVsim$id    <- factor(phenoMVsim$id)
phenoMVsim$Trial <- factor(phenoMVsim$Trial,
                           levels = paste0("Trial", 1:8))
phenoMVsim$Rep   <- factor(phenoMVsim$Rep)

4.1 Step 1 — Diagonal structure

The simplest multi-environment model assumes genetic effects in each trial are independent: a diagonal 𝐆a=diag(σg,12,…,σg,T2)\boldsymbol{G}_a = \text{diag}(\sigma^2_{g,1}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{g,T}) with no between-trial genetic correlations. This is the natural starting point.

base_diag <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
  random    = ~ diag(Trial):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Trial),
  data      = phenoMVsim,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 80
)
base_diag <- update(base_diag)

4.2 Step 2 — Factor analytic order 1

A single-factor model FA(1) introduces one set of loadings and captures the dominant axis of genotype-by-environment interaction:

base_fa1 <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
  random    = ~ fa(Trial, 1):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Trial),
  data      = phenoMVsim,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 80
)
base_fa1 <- update(base_fa1)

4.3 Step 3 — Factor analytic order 2

A two-factor model FA(2) captures two axes of interaction and provides a richer description of the genetic covariance structure. This is the model we will carry into qtlAim():

base_fa2 <- asreml(
  fixed     = yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
  random    = ~ fa(Trial, 2):id,
  residual  = ~ dsum(~units | Trial),
  data      = phenoMVsim,
  na.action = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit     = 80
)
base_fa2 <- update(base_fa2)

4.4 Model comparison

We compare the three structures using their restricted log-likelihoods. Each step adds parameters and the improvement in fit guides the choice of order:

aic <- function(mod, k) -2 * mod$loglik + 2 * k
# Parameters: diag = 8 var; fa1 = 8 psi + 8 load = 16; fa2 = 8 psi + 16 load = 24
mod_comp <- data.frame(
  Model      = c("diag(Trial)", "fa(Trial, 1)", "fa(Trial, 2)"),
  Parameters = c(8L, 16L, 24L),
  LogLik     = round(c(base_diag$loglik, base_fa1$loglik, base_fa2$loglik), 2),
  AIC        = round(c(aic(base_diag, 8), aic(base_fa1, 16), aic(base_fa2, 24)), 2)
)
print(mod_comp, row.names = FALSE)

The FA(2) model is selected as it provides the best balance between fit and parsimony while capturing two axes of genotype-by-environment interaction across the eight trials. With 8 trials, FA(2) has 24 free parameters compared to 36 for the full unstructured matrix.

5 QTL Mapping — qtlAim()

5.1 Running qtlAim()

The Trait argument activates the multivariate engine, treating "Trial" as the environment factor. Leaving str = NULL (the default) instructs qtlAim() to mirror the variance structure of the base model — here FA(2) — for the composite genome-wide random term, giving consistent modelling of the genetic covariance at every iteration without needing to respecify the order:

qtl_mv <- qtlAim(
  baseModel        = base_fa2,
  genObj           = genObj,
  merge.by         = "id",
  Trait            = "Trial",
  exclusion.window = 20,
  TypeI            = 0.05,
  trace            = FALSE,
  na.action        = na.method(x = "include"),
  maxit            = 80
)
cat("Class        :", paste(class(qtl_mv), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Engine       :", qtl_mv$QTL$path, "\n")
cat("QTL detected :", length(qtl_mv$QTL$qtl), "\n")
cat("QTL keys     :", paste(qtl_mv$QTL$qtl, collapse = ", "), "\n")

6 Results

6.1 summary() — final QTL table

The summary table reports one row per environment per detected QTL. The Trait column identifies the environment and a [MAIN] or [INT] tag (visible in print()) distinguishes QTL whose effects are consistent across environments from those with significant G×E interaction:

summ_mv <- summary(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj)
print(summ_mv)

7 Visualisation — plot()

7.1 Genome-wide outlier statistics — type = "outlier"

The outlier statistic ok=𝐪̃k⊤𝐆a−1𝐪̃k/ṽko_k = \tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k^\top \boldsymbol{G}_a^{-1}\tilde{\boldsymbol{q}}_k / \tilde{v}_k is plotted across the genome for each forward-selection iteration. Because the statistic is a quadratic form it is strictly non-negative, and its profile reveals which chromosomal regions carry the strongest multi-environment signal at each step:

plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "outlier", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.2 Scaled genome-wide BLUPs — type = "blups"

For a multivariate analysis, the BLUPs plot shows one line per trial, coloured by trial level. This display is particularly informative: intervals where all trial lines move together indicate main-effect signal, while intervals where trial lines diverge or cross indicate G×E signal:

plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "blups", sig.col = "firebrick")

7.3 Allele effects — type = "effects"

The effects lollipop is extended to show one row per trial per QTL. Main-effect QTL appear as a tight cluster of identically coloured lollipops across all trials; G×E QTL show variation in magnitude or sign across trials:

plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "effects")

7.4 Allele contrast — type = "contrast"

The contrast plot shows the total genetic value per line against its allele class at each detected QTL, separately for each trial. Main-effect QTL show the same direction of separation across all trial panels; crossover G×E QTL show the separation reversing between panels:

plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "contrast", data = phenoData, ncol = 2)

8 Iteration Diagnostics — aimTrace()

8.1 LRT trace — plot = "lrt"

The mixture chi-squared threshold (shown as a dashed line) reflects the TT-dimensional nature of the test — it lies above the univariate χ12\chi^2_1 threshold because the test jointly evaluates effects across all TT environments:

aimTrace(qtl_mv, plot = "lrt", print.out = FALSE)

8.2 Effect stability — plot = "stability"

The stability plot traces the per-trial allele effect ± 1 SE for each detected QTL across iterations. Each trial is shown as a separate coloured line. Stable main-effect QTL will show all trial lines tracking closely together; G×E QTL will show trial lines that are separated or that diverge as further QTL enter the model:

aimTrace(qtl_mv, plot = "stability", print.out = FALSE, ncol = 2)

9 Summary

The complete multivariate pipeline illustrated in this vignette is:

# 1. Prepare genotype data
genObj <- primeCross(genoMVsim, type = "interval", id = "id")

# 2. Build up the base model
base_diag <- asreml(yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
                    random = ~ diag(Trial):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Trial), data = phenoMVsim, ...)
base_fa1  <- asreml(yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
                    random = ~ fa(Trial, 1):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Trial), data = phenoMVsim, ...)
base_fa2  <- asreml(yield ~ Trial + Trial:Rep,
                    random = ~ fa(Trial, 2):id,
                    residual = ~ dsum(~units | Trial), data = phenoMVsim, ...)

# 3. Multivariate QTL mapping
qtl_mv <- qtlAim(base_fa2, genObj = genObj, merge.by = "id",
                 Trait = "Trial",
                 na.action = na.method(x = "include"), maxit = 80, ...)

# 4. Results
summary(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj)          # final QTL table (MAIN/INT)
plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "outlier")  # quadratic-form outlier stats
plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "blups")    # multi-trial BLUPs
plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "effects")  # per-trial effect lollipop
plot(qtl_mv, genObj = genObj, type = "contrast", data = phenoData, ncol = 2)
aimTrace(qtl_mv, plot = "lrt",       print.out = FALSE)
aimTrace(qtl_mv, plot = "stability", print.out = FALSE, ncol = 2)
